AutoImmune Build Plan

Oct 18, 2026 · @Pradeep

Build a hybrid pipeline: plain code for detection, validation, decisions and rollback, and an LLM only for diagnosis and patch drafting, behind a swappable provider with a no-API fallback. The research claims come from experiments, not from the demo.

# 1\. The decision

Use a hybrid pipeline. You do not need an autonomous AI agent, and you do not need to pay for anything to demo it. Only 2 of the 10 workflow steps need a model; the other 8 are ordinary code.

| **Approach**                                                    | **Cost**                                                 | **Reliability**                              | **Demo value**                                                 | **Fit for your research**                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rules only (no AI)                                              | Free                                                     | High                                         | Medium: shows detection and rollback, but nothing writes a fix | Weak: no patches to risk-score                                   |
| LLM inside a fixed pipeline                                     | Free tier or local                                       | Medium: output varies, but code validates it | High                                                           | Strong                                                           |
| Agent (the model picks tools)                                   | Free tiers run out fast, since one task makes many calls | Low: runs differ, hard to repeat or label    | High but flaky live                                            | Weak: you would measure the agent loop, not your decision policy |
| Hybrid: code for everything except diagnosis and patch drafting | Free                                                     | High                                         | High                                                           | Strong                                                           |

An agent also depends on tool calling, and one local-model guide reports parsing bugs with tool calls on the usual 8 GB coding model (qwen2.5-coder:7b; see Sources). A fixed pipeline avoids that.

### What needs AI and what does not

| **Step**                 | **Implemented as**                                 | **If no LLM is available**                                                     |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Observe, Detect          | Prometheus metrics, JSON logs, threshold rules     | Same                                                                           |
| Diagnose                 | LLM ranks causes from the stack trace and source   | Rule-based diagnoser: top project frame of the stack trace gives file and line |
| Generate repair          | LLM writes a unified diff                          | Scripted candidate pool stored in the repo                                     |
| Validate, Risk, Decide   | Docker sandbox, Maven, Semgrep and SpotBugs, rules | Same                                                                           |
| Deploy, Rollback, Record | Docker image swap, health checks, JSON files       | Same                                                                           |

### Not pretending to use AI

Put the model behind one interface with four providers: live (any hosted or local model), replay (real model output recorded earlier and served from a cache), scripted (patches your team wrote) and rule (the stack-trace diagnoser). Every saved artifact carries its provider_mode, the CLI prints a banner naming the mode, and scripted or rule-based rows are left out of any LLM repair-rate you report. That keeps a no-API demo honest.

### Language

Keep the plan you already have: Python for the pipeline, Java only for the target app. Python gives you scikit-learn, SciPy and the Docker SDK for free; a Java orchestrator adds nothing here.

### Your friend's EV project

She trains a model because the right action has to be learned from historical data. In AutoImmune, correct behaviour is defined by tests, rules and health checks, so there is nothing to learn there. The only learned part is the risk estimate, and it should be a small classical model or an empirical rate fitted on your own labelled patches (section 4), not an LSTM or any large model.

# 2\. The MVP for the 80% demo

"80% implemented" means 8 of the 10 acceptance checks below pass on demo day, each shown running, not described. Files written or code merged do not count.

| **#** | **Acceptance check**            | **Pass when**                                                                                            |
| ----- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A1    | One command runs the whole loop | python -m pipeline run --fault F06 completes on 3 different faults                                       |
| A2    | Detection                       | Incident raised within 60 s of injection; none during 5 min of healthy load                              |
| A3    | Diagnosis                       | Valid JSON with at most 3 ranked causes, provider_mode recorded, top-3 hit or miss logged whatever it is |
| A4    | Repair candidates               | 3 candidates per incident saved; each applies cleanly or is rejected with a logged reason                |
| A5    | Isolated validation             | V0 to V3 run in Docker with no network; a test proves a curl from the sandbox fails                      |
| A6    | Gates catch different things    | Across the demo faults, at least one patch is stopped by each of V1, V2 and V3                           |
| A7    | Decision                        | decision.json shows tier, decision and reasons; unit tests cover every rule                              |
| A8    | Approval path                   | An escalated patch is approved from the UI or CLI and deployed; a low-risk patch auto-applies            |
| A9    | Recovery and rollback           | A staged bad patch is rolled back automatically; a good patch is promoted                                |
| A10   | Evidence                        | analyse.py regenerates the pilot table from saved files, every number traceable                          |

### What is real and what is simplified

Steps 1 to 5 and 7 to 10 of your workflow are real. Step 6 is simplified: use a rule-based risk tier and call it a tier, not a probability. The remaining ~20% is the research layer: calibrated or empirical risk, traffic replay, mutation-gated tests, the statistical canary, the 60-fault study and baselines B1 to B3. Say exactly this to your professor.

### Failure scenarios

| **Scenario**                 | **Fault (your IDs)** | **What happens**                                                                 | **What it shows**                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| S1: wrong result             | F06 business logic   | Endpoint returns 200 with wrong data                                             | Detection needs a content check, because error rate and health stay green; V1 catches a patch that does not fix it |
| S2: regression               | F01 null error       | A candidate stops the crash by returning an empty result and breaks another test | V1 passes, V2 rejects                                                                                              |
| S3a: unhealthy service       | F04 config           | Wrong property: health goes DOWN                                                 | Detection by health rule, deploy with health window                                                                |
| S3b: bad patch escapes gates | Staged candidate     | Passes all tests but adds a 3 s delay on a path no test covers                   | Deploy, p95 breaches 2 s, automatic rollback                                                                       |
| S4: insecure patch           | Candidate for F05    | Fix built from string-concatenated SQL                                           | V3 rejects                                                                                                         |

Build S1, S2 and S3 first (faults F06, F01, F04): between them they exercise every gate and the rollback path. Treat S4 as a candidate in the pool, not a separate fault. Add F02, F03 and F05 afterwards.

### Two fixes to your existing 7-day plan

- **Detector (Step 10).** Your rules (5xx share, p95, health) will not fire on F05 or F06, which return 200. Add a probe rule: every 10 s call 3 known endpoints, compare with expected values, raise an incident after 2 mismatches in a row. That is real code, not AI.
- **Candidate pool.** For each demo fault, write 4 candidates by hand in faults/&lt;id&gt;/candidates/: correct, overfitting, regressive, insecure. Mark them scripted. Without them, a strong model fixes your simple bugs correctly and the decision engine has nothing to decide. Report scripted results separately from LLM results: they test your validation pipeline, not the model.

If you fall behind, cut in this order: Grafana (use the Prometheus UI), the web approval page (use a CLI prompt), SpotBugs (keep Semgrep in V3).

# 3\. System architecture

One Python orchestrator runs a fixed sequence of ten steps. Each step reads one artifact and writes one artifact, so any run can be replayed, audited and counted. The model is called in steps 3 and 4 only.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. Architecture: data and decisions flow top to bottom; the orchestrator writes every step to evidence.jsonl.

Mermaid source (paste into a README or mermaid.live):

```
flowchart LR
  A["Spring Boot order-service<br/>(Docker)"] -->|"metrics + JSON logs"| D["Detector<br/>thresholds + probe rule"]
  D -->|"incident.json"| G["Orchestrator<br/>(Python, fixed sequence)"]
  G --> P["Provider layer<br/>live / replay / scripted / rule"]
  P -->|"diagnosis.json +<br/>3 candidate diffs"| S["Sandbox: Docker, no network<br/>gates V0 to V3"]
  S -->|"gates.json"| R{"Decision engine<br/>tier + reasons"}
  R -->|"REJECT"| X["Rejected,<br/>try next candidate"]
  R -->|"ESCALATE"| H["Human approval<br/>(CLI or UI)"]
  R -->|"AUTO_APPLY"| DEP["Deploy: image swap<br/>+ health window"]
  H -->|"approve"| DEP
  DEP -->|"breach"| RB["Rollback to<br/>previous image"]
  DEP -->|"healthy"| OK["Promote"]
  G -.-> E[("evidence.jsonl<br/>runs/run_id/")]
```

## 3.1 Components

| **Component**     | **Technology**                                                            | **Responsibility**                                                                               |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Target app        | Java 17, Spring Boot 3, Maven, Actuator, Micrometer                       | Order service carrying six source-level faults. Each fault has a reference fix and hidden tests. |
| Detector          | Python; Prometheus scrape; JSON logs                                      | Threshold rules (5xx share, p95, health) plus the probe rule for faults that return 200.         |
| Provider layer    | Python interface; modes live, replay, scripted, rule                      | Diagnose and draft patches. Nothing else calls a model.                                          |
| Sandbox           | Docker with --network none; prebuilt image with Maven dependencies cached | Runs gates V0 to V3 on a copy of the source with resource limits and timeouts.                   |
| Decision engine   | Python, pure functions                                                    | Turns gate results into tier, decision and reasons.                                              |
| Deploy controller | Docker image swap; health window                                          | Promote, approval path, automatic rollback.                                                      |
| Evidence store    | JSON file per run; one evidence.jsonl table                               | Single source for every reported number.                                                         |
| Analysis          | pandas, SciPy                                                             | analyse.py: tables, confidence intervals, policy comparisons.                                    |

## 3.3 Validation gates

| **Gate** | **Runs**                                          | **What it is meant to catch**                                                                            |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| V0       | Apply the diff, mvn compile                       | Diffs that do not apply or do not build                                                                  |
| V1       | Target test that reproduces the fault             | Patches that do not fix the fault                                                                        |
| V2       | Full existing test suite                          | Regressions (S2).                                                                                        |
| V3       | Semgrep security rules, SpotBugs with FindSecBugs | Insecure fixes (S4) and bug patterns. Findings are counted only if new compared with the unpatched code. |

Hidden tests are never mounted in the sandbox. They exist only to label patches afterwards (section 4.4). Traffic replay and mutation-gated tests are research-layer additions and are not part of the MVP gates.

## 3.4 Decision rules (version 1, rule-based tier)

| **Tier** | **Condition**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | **Decision**        |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| High     | Any gate V0 to V2 fails, or a new high-severity security finding appears in V3                                                                                                                                                                             | REJECT              |
| Medium   | All gates pass, but at least one of: new low-severity finding; diff larger than the size limit; diff touches a file other than the diagnosed one; diff touches configuration or security-sensitive paths; diagnosis samples disagree (live or replay only) | ESCALATE to a human |
| Low      | All gates pass, no new findings, diff inside the diagnosed file and within the size limit                                                                                                                                                                  | AUTO_APPLY          |

The tier is an ordered label, not a probability. The size limit and any other numeric threshold are fixed on the development faults before the test faults are run, and each rule has a unit test (A7).

## 3.5 Deploy and rollback

- **Deploy:** build an image from the patched source, start it next to the running one, and watch it for the health window before it takes traffic.
- **Health window passes when:** /actuator/health stays UP, p95 stays under 2 s, and probe responses match expected values for the whole window.
- **Rollback:** on any breach, swap back to the previous image tag and write a rollback event. Use an image swap, not git checkout, so the running service always matches a known build.
- **Reject is not rollback:** reject happens before deploy and is a decision; rollback happens after deploy and is a recovery. Record them as separate events.

## 3.6 Repository layout

```
autoimmune/
  app/                     Spring Boot order-service (healthy code)
  faults/F01..F06/         fault.json, reference.diff, target_test/, hidden_tests/,
                           candidates/ (scripted: correct, overfitting, regressive, insecure)
  pipeline/                detector, providers, sandbox, decide, deploy, record
  config/decision.yaml     size limit and other thresholds
  cache/                   recorded model outputs for replay mode
  runs/<run_id>/           incident, diagnosis, candidates, gates, decision, deploy, health
  evidence.jsonl           one row per candidate
  analyse.py               regenerates every table

```

# 4\. Research contribution

## 4.1 Framing

AutoImmune is the instrument, and the study is a measurement: how often do test-passing AI patches turn out unsafe, and what does each additional check buy. Build the patch pool once, store one evidence row per patch, and treat every deployment policy as a function over those rows. Thresholds and cost ratios can then be swept in pandas without re-running anything. A null or negative result is still a finding, which a "calibrated deployer" claim cannot say.

## 4.2 Gaps and research questions

Each gap has the form "existing work does X, but we found no study of Y". Say "to the best of our literature search" on the slide.

| **#** | **Nearest existing work**                                                                                                                                                                                      | **What we did not find**                                                                                                                       | **Research question**                                                                                                                   |
| ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| G1    | Google's agentic repair paper (Abstain and Validate, ICSE-SEIP 2026) filters bugs and patches before review, but a human still reviews each patch. Meta's Diff Risk Score gates human-written diffs.           | A measurement of when human review of an LLM patch can be skipped, using execution evidence and a stated cost.                                 | RQ1: With what evidence can review be skipped while the unsafe-deployment rate among auto-applied patches stays at or below a target α? |
| G2    | Calibration studies of code LLMs address the model's own confidence, including repair; fine-grained Platt scaling has been applied to code-revision confidence.                                                | Gate results (build, tests, scans) turned into a calibrated probability that a patch is unsafe, with a cost-based decision rule.               | RQ2: How well do gate results predict an unsafe patch, and is a calibrated probability achievable at our data size?                     |
| G3    | One SWE-Bench analysis found overfitting patches inflate resolution rates by 6.2 points on average. Work on LLM patch-correctness judging and LLM-generated assertions (ComPass, FixCheck) reports weaknesses. | A measurement of what each validation level catches and costs for LLM repair patches, in unsafe patches deployed against human reviews needed. | RQ3: What does each level V0 to V3 catch, at what time cost?                                                                            |

### Hypothesis H1 (diagnosis uncertainty)

We hypothesize that low agreement between repeated diagnosis samples predicts an unsafe patch. This is our inference, not a published finding. ORCA-bench, a vendor benchmark, reports frequent wrong root causes for frontier models, which motivates the test. H1 needs live or replay output; scripted and rule-based rows have no diagnosis confidence and are excluded.

## 4.3 Related work to name on the slide

- Google, Abstain and Validate (arXiv 2510.03217): closest to G1.
- Meta, Diff Risk Score: risk gating for human-written diffs.
- Spiess et al., Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code; fine-grained confidence calibration in code revision: closest to G2.
- Durieux et al., Production-Driven Patch Generation: shadow-traffic testing of patches. Traffic replay is therefore a component here, not a contribution.
- ORCA (arXiv 2608.17018): telemetry-grounded patch verification. We concede that verification is not new.
- HealBench (arXiv 2609.39086): only a snippet was seen and it looks close to the trust theme. Read it before the viva.

## 4.4 Ground truth

A patch is labelled unsafe if any of the following holds. The labels come from the team, are written before any policy is run, and are never visible to the gates.

- It fails the hidden behavioural tests for its fault (more cases than the visible target test).
- An exploit test confirms an injection or similar weakness it introduces.
- It breaches the health window in a deploy (health, p95, probe mismatch). Note: the staged S3b patch is built to breach, so its rollback demonstrates that the mechanism works. It is not a measured catch rate; record it with staged=true and report real rollback catches separately.
- It breaks a reference regression probe that the visible suite does not cover.

label_source records which rule fired. Disputed cases are labelled by two team members. Correct patches that are rejected count toward false rejection.

## 4.5 Risk estimate, in stages

| **Stage**               | **What it is**                                                                                                                                                                          | **What you may call it**                               |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1 (MVP)                 | Rule-based tier from section 3.4                                                                                                                                                        | A risk tier                                            |
| 2                       | Empirical unsafe rate per evidence pattern (for example V0 to V3 pass, no new findings), with a Wilson 95% interval. Auto-apply only patterns whose upper bound is at most α.           | An empirical risk estimate                             |
| 3 (only if data allows) | Logistic regression on gate features, evaluated by reliability table and Brier score. A common rule of thumb asks for about 10 unsafe patches per feature; with fewer, stay at stage 2. | Calibrated, and only if the reliability table shows it |

Cost-based rule: with cost C_u for an unsafe deploy and C_r for a human review, auto-apply when P(unsafe) × C_u is below C_r, otherwise escalate; gate failures are rejected outright. Report results over a range of C_u / C_r rather than one chosen value. If calibration is not reached, report the AUROC of the tier against the labels as the fallback.

## 4.6 What we claim and what we do not

| **We claim**                                                           | **We do not claim**                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A labelled evidence set of AI patches and what each gate caught        | That we are the first to verify AI patches (ORCA does)                        |
| A measured comparison of policies B0 to B3 on that set, with intervals | That we are the first to roll back after deploy (canary analysis is standard) |
| Per-gate catch and cost figures                                        | That traffic replay is new (Durieux et al.)                                   |
| A pilot result at MVP size, labelled as a pilot                        | A calibrated probability, unless stage 3 shows it                             |
| Results for one Java service                                           | That results generalise beyond it                                             |

### One-line gap statement for the slide

"Existing work generates and verifies LLM patches, but humans still review every patch. To the best of our literature search, no study measures how much execution evidence lets an AI patch deploy without a human, at a stated cost."

# 5\. Experimental evaluation

## 5.1 Patch pool

| **Stage**      | **Size**                                | **Candidates per fault**               | **What you may claim**                             |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Pilot (25 Oct) | 6 faults                                | 3 (18 patches)                         | A pilot run with counts only; no inference         |
| Full study     | Up to 15 faults: 5 development, 10 test | 4 scripted + 3 LLM (up to 105 patches) | Rates with confidence intervals on the test faults |
| Optional       | A few real Java bugs from Defects4J     | LLM only                               | Reduces single-app bias; report separately         |

- Scripted rows (correct, overfitting, regressive, insecure) test the validation pipeline. LLM rows test the model. Report them separately, and report hand-written unsafe candidates separately from LLM-produced ones.
- A strong model fixes simple bugs correctly, so unsafe LLM patches may be rare. That is why the scripted pool exists; state the prevalence you observed.
- Run each live diagnosis 3 times and record model name, temperature and date. After that, rerun from the replay cache.

## 5.2 Baselines

| **ID**              | **Policy**             | **Rule**                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| B0                  | Universal human review | Every patch is escalated, so nothing is auto-applied and UDR is undefined (no auto-applied patches). HIR is 100%. B0 is the reference point for reviews removed, assuming a perfect reviewer; it is not a measured result. |
| B1                  | Test-only gate         | Auto-apply if V0 and V1 pass; otherwise reject.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| B2                  | Fixed rules            | Auto-apply if V0 to V2 pass; otherwise reject. No static analysis (that is V3).                                                                                                                                            |
| B3                  | AutoImmune tier        | V0 to V3 (including new static findings) and the three-way rules in section 3.4.                                                                                                                                           |
| B4 (research layer) | Empirical-risk policy  | Stage 2 of section 4.5, optionally with diagnosis agreement.                                                                                                                                                               |

All baselines are computed from the same evidence rows, so every policy sees identical patches and nothing is re-run.

## 5.3 Metrics

| **Metric**                   | **Definition**                                                                 | **Note**                                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| UDR, unsafe deployment rate  | Auto-applied patches labelled unsafe ÷ auto-applied patches                    | Report the count; undefined if nothing is auto-applied                                                                          |
| HIR, human intervention rate | Escalated patches ÷ all patches                                                | Reviews removed = 100% minus HIR, compared with B0                                                                              |
| FRR, false rejection rate    | Safe, valid patches rejected ÷ all safe, valid patches                         | Measures what over-caution costs                                                                                                |
| Gate catch and cost          | For each gate: unsafe patches first stopped there, and seconds spent           | Section 5.5                                                                                                                     |
| Rollback catch               | Unsafe patches that passed all gates and were rolled back in the health window | Real catches only. Staged S3b runs are a demonstration of the mechanism and are tagged staged=true and excluded from this rate. |
| Recovery time                | Detection to healthy service                                                   | Seconds, from saved timestamps                                                                                                  |

## 5.4 Statistics at small sample sizes

- Report proportions with Wilson 95% intervals, never bare percentages.
- **Rule of three:** if zero of n auto-applied patches are unsafe, the 95% upper bound on UDR is about 3/n. Showing UDR below α = 0.05 therefore needs about 60 auto-applied patches with none unsafe. The pilot cannot show this and must not claim it.
- Patches of the same fault are correlated, so compare policies with a bootstrap that resamples faults, not patches.
- Fix thresholds on the development faults, then evaluate once on the test faults.

## 5.5 Validation depth analysis

For every unsafe patch, record the first gate that stops it. The table of unsafe patches caught per gate, with seconds spent per gate, answers RQ3 and shows the cost of each extra level. A gate that never stops anything unique is a finding too.

## 5.6 Threats to validity

| **Threat**                                       | **How it is handled**                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scripted candidates are written by the team      | Reported separately from LLM rows; described as tests of the pipeline                   |
| Hidden tests and labels written by the same team | Labels fixed before policies run; double labelling of disputes; optional Defects4J bugs |
| One small Java service                           | Stated as a limit; no claim of generality                                               |
| LLM output varies between runs                   | Three runs, recorded settings, replay cache                                             |
| Small N                                          | Intervals, rule of three, pilot label                                                   |
| B0 assumes a perfect reviewer                    | Stated; B0 is a reference point                                                         |

# 6\. Infrastructure and cost

Everything runs on one laptop at no cost. The design assumption is that no external service is needed on demo day.

| **Item**                  | **Choice**                                            | **Note**                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hosted model              | Any provider with a free tier                         | Limits below were checked on 18 Oct 2026 from third-party pages. Confirm in the provider console on the day.          |
| Local model               | Ollama with qwen2.5-coder:7b                          | Runs offline. The pipeline does not use tool calling, so the tool-call parsing issue in section 1 does not apply.     |
| Replay cache              | Key = hash of provider, model, prompt and temperature | One real call per prompt. Experiments and demos then read the cache and cost nothing.                                 |
| Scripted and rule modes   | Files in the repository                               | Last-resort fallback; always labelled in the banner.                                                                  |
| Machine                   | Laptop with Docker Desktop                            | 16 GB RAM is recommended if the local model and Docker run together (our recommendation, not a measured requirement). |
| Security and static tools | Semgrep, SpotBugs, Maven                              | Free and open source.                                                                                                 |
| Metrics and dashboards    | Prometheus; Grafana only if time allows               | The Prometheus UI is enough for the demo.                                                                             |

## Free hosted options (checked 18 Oct 2026)

- Figures come from third-party pages and change often; the provider console is authoritative. All are per-project or per-organisation limits, so one team account shares them.

| **Provider**                   | **Free-tier limit (as reported)**                                                 | **Caveat**                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| OpenRouter, :free models       | 20 requests/min; 50 requests/day, or 1,000/day after a one-time \$10 top-up       | The list of free models rotates. A negative balance returns HTTP 402.                                 |
| Groq, free plan                | Per-model limits, e.g. 30 RPM, 1,000 RPD, 8,000 TPM, 200,000 TPD for gpt-oss-120b | Check the console for the model you pick. Limits apply per organisation.                              |
| Google Gemini, free tier       | Per-project, per-model limits shown in AI Studio                                  | One third-party doc says about 5 to 10 RPM for Flash models; the official numbers were not confirmed. |
| Ollama, local qwen2.5-coder:7b | No request limits; about 4.7 GB download                                          | About 8 GB RAM or VRAM minimum. Runs offline.                                                         |

- Call budget: with a replay cache the pipeline needs one real call per prompt. 3 candidates + 1 diagnosis per fault across 6 faults is about 24 calls plus repeats for the agreement test, well inside any limit above. Record each real call once, then replay.

## Sandbox practicalities

- Build the sandbox image once with all Maven dependencies cached, then run with --network none. Without this, offline builds fail.
- Set CPU and memory limits and a timeout per gate, so a hung build cannot stall the run.
- Mount a copy of the source, not the working tree, and never mount hidden tests.

## Risks and fallbacks

| **Risk**                            | **Fallback**                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hosted model quota or network fails | Switch to local model, then replay, then scripted; the banner names the mode                    |
| Docker or Maven is slow on demo day | Pre-warm the image; run gates on cached builds; rehearse the full run                           |
| A scenario behaves differently live | Every decision is computed, so show the evidence and explain; keep recorded runs from rehearsal |
| Time runs short                     | Apply the cut order from section 2                                                              |

At the end of each day the check for that day must run, not just be written. Commit and tag the passing state so there is always a working version to fall back to.

If time runs short, drop R4 items from the bottom first. A labelled pool with B0 to B3 and honest intervals (R1 to R3) is the core contribution.

## 8.3 Likely questions

| **Question**                       | **Answer**                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Why not an autonomous agent?       | An agent makes many calls, varies between runs and is hard to label. We measure the deploy policy, so only diagnosis and drafting use a model. |
| Is the demo scripted?              | The scripted candidates are test inputs, labelled scripted and reported separately. Every decision is computed from gate results.              |
| How do you know a patch is unsafe? | Labels from hidden tests, exploit tests and staged deploys, written independently of the gates (section 4.4).                                  |
| What is new?                       | The gap statement in section 4.2. We do not claim first verification, first rollback or new traffic replay.                                    |
| Is the risk score calibrated?      | No. At MVP it is a rule-based tier. We report an empirical estimate, and calibration only if the data supports it.                             |
| What if the model is unavailable?  | Replay, then scripted modes, named in the banner.                                                                                              |
| Is 18 patches enough?              | No, and we call it a pilot. Section 5.4 shows what sample size the target rate needs.                                                          |
| What is the remaining 20%?         | Empirical or calibrated risk, traffic replay, mutation-gated tests, statistical canary, the larger study and baselines B1 to B3.               |

# 9\. Prompt templates for AI coding assistants

Use one prompt per module. Paste the context block first, run the acceptance check, and paste any failure back before moving on. Commit each passing step. The team writes the labels, the hidden tests and the expected values; the assistant must not, and every reported number must trace to evidence.jsonl.

**Context block (paste at the start of every prompt)**

Project: AutoImmune, a hybrid self-healing pipeline for a Java Spring Boot service. Python 3.11 orchestrator; Java only for the target app.

Design rules: fixed pipeline, no agent loops, no tool calling. A model is used only to diagnose and to draft patches, behind a provider interface with modes live, replay, scripted and rule. Every artifact is JSON and carries provider_mode. Scripted and rule rows are never counted as LLM results.

Risk output is a rule-based tier (low, medium, high), not a probability. Hidden tests are never visible to the gates. Keep modules small and add pytest tests.

**Prompt 1: target app and faults**

Create a Spring Boot 3, Java 17, Maven service "order-service" with GET /api/orders, an order total endpoint, a discount endpoint, Actuator health and a Prometheus metrics endpoint, plus a healthy test suite.

Add six faults F01 to F06 as real source-level bugs, each on its own branch with: fault.json (description), reference.diff (the correct fix), a visible target test that fails on the bug, and a hidden_tests folder. Required first: F06 business logic returning 200 with wrong data, F01 null error, F04 wrong configuration property that turns health DOWN. F05 must return 200 and use string-built SQL. Use the team fault table for F02 and F03.

Do not use runtime fault toggles. Acceptance: mvn test passes on healthy code; each fault is reproduced by its target test.

**Prompt 2: detector**

Write detector.py. Scrape Prometheus metrics and read JSON logs. Rules: 5xx share, p95 latency, health DOWN. Add a probe rule: every 10 s call 3 known endpoints, compare with expected values, raise an incident after 2 mismatches in a row. Write incident.json with timestamp, rule fired, evidence and stack trace if any.

Acceptance: incident within 60 s of injecting F06 and F04; no incident during 5 minutes of healthy load; pytest covers each rule.

**Prompt 3: provider layer**

Write a Provider interface with diagnose(incident, source) -> Diagnosis and draft_patch(diagnosis, source, n=3) -> list of Patch. Implement modes live (configurable hosted or Ollama endpoint), replay (cache keyed by hash of provider, model, prompt, temperature), scripted (reads faults/&lt;id&gt;/candidates/) and rule (top project stack frame gives file and line).

Validate diagnosis against a JSON schema with at most 3 ranked causes; retry at most twice. Check each diff with git apply --check and log the reason if it fails. Print a banner naming the mode and write provider_mode into every artifact.

Acceptance: A3 and A4 from the plan, including a test that replay mode makes no network call.

**Prompt 4: sandbox gates**

Write sandbox.py with run_gates(patch) -> gates.json. Use Docker with --network none, a prebuilt image with Maven dependencies cached, CPU and memory limits, a timeout per gate, and a copy of the source (never the hidden tests). V0: apply and compile. V1: target test. V2: full existing test suite. V3: Semgrep and SpotBugs with FindSecBugs. For V3 count only findings that are new compared with the unpatched code, with severity. Record seconds per gate.

Acceptance: a test proves curl from inside the sandbox fails; across the demo faults at least one patch is stopped by each of V1, V2 and V3.

**Prompt 5: decision engine**

Write decide.py as pure functions: decide(gates, diagnosis, config) -> Decision with tier, decision (AUTO_APPLY, ESCALATE, REJECT) and a list of reasons. Rules: reject if any of V0 to V2 fails or a new high-severity finding exists; escalate if all gates pass but there is a new low-severity finding, an oversized diff, a diff outside the diagnosed file or in configuration or security-sensitive paths, or low diagnosis agreement; otherwise auto-apply. Read thresholds from config/decision.yaml.

Acceptance: pytest covers every rule branch and every reason string.

**Prompt 6: deploy, approval and rollback**

Write deploy.py. Build an image from the patched source, start it beside the running one, and watch a health window: /actuator/health UP, p95 under 2 s, probes matching expected values. On pass, promote; on any breach, swap back to the previous image tag and write a rollback event. Add a CLI approval prompt that shows the diff, tier and reasons, with approve and reject. Keep reject (before deploy) and rollback (after deploy) as separate events.

Acceptance: A8 and A9, including a staged patch that passes all gates, adds a 3 s delay on an untested path, and is rolled back automatically.

**Prompt 7: evidence and analysis**

Write record.py to append one row per candidate to evidence.jsonl with the fields in section 3.7. Write analyse.py to regenerate: counts per decision, unsafe patches caught per gate with seconds, and UDR, HIR and FRR for B0 to B3 computed as functions over the rows, with Wilson 95% intervals and the number of rows behind each figure. Report scripted and LLM rows separately.

Acceptance: A10. Deleting the tables and rerunning analyse.py reproduces them exactly.
